stances.claim: Amid sad news -- coronavirus surge, PhilHealth plunder, Jolo blasts, Duterte's health disclosure -- three pieces of 'shiny good news' deserve recognition: Duterte's RevGov disavowal, COVID curve flattening, and more aggressive WPS assertion.

Duterte's firm RevGov disavowal -- backed by DefSec Lorenzana ('illegal and unconstitutional') and FS Locsin ('unique in its insanity') -- settles the question because 'No RevGov is possible without the military's backing,' as Cory Aquino's 1986 set-aside of the 1973 Constitution succeeded only with people-and-military support that's now absent. IBP president Cayosa's push to charge RevGov promoters with 'inciting to sedition' is correct, 'subject to the caveat that facts must be proven according to the rules of evidence, not necessarily according to media reports.'

The COVID-19 curve is flattening per UP OCTA Research Team's Prof. Guido David -- but his caveat is dispositive: 'flattening does not mean it is over. It means there are still cases but the [TRANSMISSION RATE] is on the decline. Flattening is a long process.' As more asymptomatic carriers return to offices, malls, and normal life, 'the chances of contact surge,' requiring continued vigilance on isolation, distancing, face masks/shields, and hand-washing.

The third good news is a more aggressive WPS posture led by Lorenzana and Locsin -- DFA diplomatic protest over Chinese Coast Guard's 'illegal confiscation' of Filipino fishing equipment near Scarborough Shoal; Lorenzana's debunking of the 'nine-dash line' as 'fabrication' and his 'illegally occupying' charge against Beijing; Roque's affirmation of supply missions to the Spratlys and overflights in Scarborough -- yet with the 12-mile Duterte standing order limiting PH naval involvement to 'our national waters.'

The US-China 'war of nerves and tech' is escalating -- Azar's Taiwan visit, China's fighters across the median maritime line Aug. 10, the US $66-unit F-16C-D sale Aug. 20, China's SCS missile firings demonstrating warship-sink capability, US sanctions on 24 SCS-construction Chinese companies (one a MacroAsia partner on the $10-billion Sangley Point International Airport) -- and Malaysia's FM Hishammuddin Hussein is right that Asean must get together to avoid being 'dragged and trapped' between the two superpowers.

PH should 'neither be pro-American nor pro-Chinese. Rather, we should always be pro-Filipino and align ourselves with our Asean brethren in dealing with the two giants.' This is the operational doctrine that reconciles the WPS-pushback (against China) with the non-participation in US-led SCS exercises (independent of US).

notable_anecdotes: The sorting-good-from-sad opening device -- itemizing four sad-news items (coronavirus, PhilHealth plunder, Jolo blasts, Duterte's Barrett's-esophagus warning) before pivoting to three good-news items -- gives the column its title structure and its measured emotional register.

The Lorenzana-Locsin twin condemnation of RevGov -- 'illegal and unconstitutional' (DefSec) and 'unique in its insanity' (FS) -- quoted in tandem to demonstrate cabinet-level consensus across two of Duterte's strongest departments.

The historical-analogy reassurance -- Cory Aquino's 1986 set-aside of the 1973 Constitution 'succeeded because our people, backed up by the military, supported it' -- making explicit why current RevGov efforts lack the foundational condition (military backing) for success.
Prof. Guido David's caveat preserved verbatim -- 'Flattening is a long process' -- used as the dispositive science-relay that prevents premature relief.
Lorenzana's 'fabrication' attack on the nine-dash line -- a defense-secretary-level escalation of WPS language from 'disputed' to 'illegally occupying' that signals administration-line hardening.

Duterte's '12-mile standing order' as quoted by Lorenzana -- 'we should not involve ourselves in naval exercises in the [SCS] except in our national waters, the 12-mile distance from our shores' -- explaining PH's non-participation in US-led exercises in operational specifics.

The Sangley Point International Airport contract review -- Locsin's plan to terminate government contracts with US-sanctioned Chinese companies (one a $10-billion MacroAsia partner) -- making the US-China escalation's financial-stake bite at the PH infrastructure level.
The Malaysian FM Hishammuddin Hussein quote -- Asean must avoid being 'dragged and trapped' -- anchoring CJ's pro-Filipino-and-pro-Asean prescription in a regional foreign-minister's own framing.
The Aug. 10 / Aug. 20 / 66 F-16 / 24 sanctioned companies sequence -- making the US-China escalation chronology audit-able by specific dates and counts.
CJ's tri-stance closer -- 'neither pro-American nor pro-Chinese' but 'pro-Filipino' aligned with Asean -- distilling the column's geopolitical doctrine into a single declarative sentence.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban sorts the good news from the sad. The sad: the 'worrying rise in the ABSOLUTE NUMBER of coronavirus infections,' the 'shocking plunder of PhilHealth funds,' the 'deadly Jolo blasts,' and the President's revelation that his doctors warned his Barrett's esophagus 'may worsen to Stage One cancer.' Against this, he welcomes three 'shiny good news' items. First, Duterte's firm disavowal of RevGov: Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana declared it 'illegal and unconstitutional' and Foreign Secretary Teodoro Locsin Jr. condemned it as 'unique in its insanity.' IBP president Domingo Egon Cayosa wants to charge RevGov promoters with 'inciting to sedition'; CJ agrees, 'subject to the caveat that facts must be proven according to the rules of evidence, not necessarily according to media reports.' Historically, 'No RevGov is possible without the military's backing': Cory Aquino's 1986 set-aside of the 1973 Constitution succeeded only 'because our people, backed up by the military, supported it' before the 1987 Constitution took effect a year later -- current RevGov efforts lack that foundational condition. Second, the flattening of the COVID-19 curve per UP OCTA Research Team's Prof. Guido David, with his dispositive caveat: 'flattening does not mean it is over. It means there are still cases but the [TRANSMISSION RATE] is on the decline. Flattening is a long process.' As asymptomatic carriers return to offices, malls, and normal life, 'the chances of contact surge,' requiring continued isolation, physical distancing, face masks and shields, and hand-washing. Third, a more aggressive assertion of WPS maritime rights led by Lorenzana and Locsin: a DFA diplomatic protest over the Chinese Coast Guard's 'illegal confiscation' of Filipino fishermen's equipment near Scarborough Shoal; Lorenzana's debunking of China's 'nine-dash line' as 'fabrication' and accusation of Beijing 'illegally occupying' PH maritime territory; Palace spokesperson Harry Roque's affirmation that military movements in the WPS align with sovereign rights and that supply missions in the Spratlys and overflights in Scarborough will continue. Yet PH refused to join the US Navy's recent 'world's largest maritime military exercises' in the SCS -- Lorenzana citing Duterte's standing order: 'we should not involve ourselves in naval exercises in the [SCS] except in our national waters, the 12-mile distance from our shores.' Meanwhile, the US-China 'war of nerves and tech' escalates: US Health Secretary Alex Azar visited Taiwan; on August 10 China flew fighter planes across the median maritime line separating the mainland from Taiwan; on August 20 the US sold 66 ultra-hi-tech F-16C-D fighter jets to Taiwan; China fired missiles into the SCS showing it could sink US warships; and the US imposed sanctions on 24 Chinese companies that constructed the artificial islands in the SCS. Locsin said he would ask for termination of government contracts with the sanctioned companies -- one of which (with MacroAsia Corp.) was awarded the $10-billion Sangley Point International Airport build. Roque hoped the US and China would resolve their disputes 'amicably and peacefully,' and Malaysian FM Datuk Seri Hishammuddin Hussein was clearer: Asean countries must get together to avoid being 'dragged and trapped' between the two superpowers. CJ closes: 'we should neither be pro-American nor pro-Chinese. Rather, we should always be pro-Filipino and align ourselves with our Asean brethren in dealing with the two giants.'
